title: Quantum electrodynamics: how electrons and photons interact
text: Quantum electrodynamics covers one thing: how electrons, positrons and photons exchange energy and momentum. Draw every possible interaction as a Feynman diagram, give each a complex amplitude, and add them; each extra vertex multiplies by e≈0.303, so a few orders already give high precision. QED contains neither the strong force nor gravity, and it does not explain why the electron has mass.

title: Path integrals: every possible path carries a little arrow
text: Feynman taught quantum mechanics with arrows: an event's amplitude is an arrow whose direction is the action divided by hbar. A particle going from A to B contributes one arrow per path; join them head to tail and square the length for the probability. Near the classical path the arrows line up and add; elsewhere they cancel, which is why an apple seems to take a single route.

title: A Feynman diagram is not a picture of a trajectory
text: A Feynman diagram is a way of writing an integral; the horizontal axis is not time. External lines are the given particles, internal lines are integrated over all four-momenta, and every vertex is one interaction conserving charge and momentum. Internal lines may look faster than light or backward in time: that is bookkeeping, not an observable track. Read a diagram by counting vertices, not as billiard balls.

title: An antiparticle is an electron running backward in time
text: Feynman and Stueckelberg gave the picture: a positron can be read as an electron moving backward along time. In quantum field theory this is not a mere metaphor; the propagator depends on the spacetime interval, so negative-energy solutions become positrons with consistent charge and energy. The picture predicts pair creation and annihilation, and experiment agrees.
aliases: why is the positron an electron going backward in time

title: Renormalization is not sweeping infinities under the rug
text: Electron self-energy and vacuum polarization produce infinities. Renormalization admits that bare charge and bare mass are not observables: absorb the infinities into those definitions and compare only the finite corrections with experiment. Feynman disliked it at first, since it looked like hiding the problem, but he accepted that it is the only scheme that reproduces eleven-digit agreement.

title: The electron g factor is not exactly 2
text: The Dirac equation gives an electron magnetic moment of two Bohr magnetons, but the measured value is 2(1+a) with a≈0.001159652. This anomalous moment comes from the electron interacting with its own field; QED computes it order by order, and the fifth-order result matches experiment to eleven significant digits, the tightest agreement in physics.
aliases: why is the electron moment not 2

title: Vacuum polarization and the Lamb shift
text: The vacuum is not empty: virtual electron-positron pairs briefly screen charge, which is vacuum polarization. It splits the hydrogen 2S and 2P levels by about 1057 MHz, the Lamb shift measured in 1947. QED got that small shift right, and only then did physicists take the theory seriously.

title: The force between two electrons is virtual-photon exchange
text: In QED two electrons interact by exchanging virtual photons. A virtual photon has k² not equal to zero, so no detector can catch one; it exists only as the mediator. More exchanges and closer approach mean larger corrections, and those loop diagrams produce the Lamb shift and g-2.

title: 1/137 makes QED work, and makes it fail in strong fields
text: The fine-structure constant is about 1/137, so each extra vertex costs e≈0.303. Because the coupling is small, a few orders already give high precision, which is why QED is so usable. Near the critical field of 1.3×10¹⁸ V/m the expansion breaks down and the vacuum itself can pair-produce.

title: The photon has no rest mass, and that is why c is the limit
text: A nonzero photon mass would make Coulomb's law short-ranged, make light speed depend on frequency, and break gauge invariance; experiment bounds it below about 10⁻¹⁸ eV. Feynman stressed that c is not merely the speed of light but a constant of spacetime: a photon travels at c because it is massless.

title: Nuclear force comes from meson exchange, but that is not the whole strong force
text: Yukawa explained the nuclear force in 1935 by exchanging mesons: the range is about hbar divided by mc, and a pion mass of 140 MeV gives roughly 1.4 fm. That picture captures short range, strength and saturation, but pion exchange is only the residual strong force; the real mediators are gluons, and the pion is a quark-antiquark pair.

title: Partons: hitting a proton with electrons hits nearly free points
text: Deep inelastic scattering at SLAC in 1968 showed that high-energy electrons scatter off the proton as if it were a set of nearly free, pointlike objects rather than a smooth charge cloud. Feynman called them partons and predicted scaling. They turned out to be quarks and gluons; scaling breaks at low energy because gluons are emitted.

title: Asymptotic freedom and confinement are two ends of one coupling
text: The strong coupling shrinks as energy rises, so at high energy quarks look nearly free; at low energy the coupling grows and quarks stay locked inside hadrons. Pull a quark hard enough and the energy creates a quark-antiquark pair from the vacuum, so the string breaks into two hadrons instead of yielding one free quark.

title: The weak force: slow, short-ranged, and able to change particle type
text: Beta decay is mediated by the weak force, about a dozen orders of magnitude weaker than the strong force and far shorter in range. Feynman and Gell-Mann proposed the V minus A theory in 1958: the weak current is vector minus axial vector, which explains both parity violation and the similar shapes of muon and neutron decay.

title: Parity violation: the bet Feynman lost
text: In 1956 Lee and Yang suggested the weak interaction might not conserve space inversion. In 1957 Wu's team saw electrons from cobalt-60 emitted preferentially opposite the nuclear spin, confirming the violation. Feynman had bet on parity being conserved and lost. His lesson: symmetry is settled by experiment, not by how it ought to look.

title: Neutrinos barely interact with anything
text: A neutrino feels only the weak force and has a tiny mass. Electron neutrinos from the Sun cross the Earth like air; stopping half of them needs about a light-year of lead. Neutrino oscillations were confirmed long after Feynman, proving they have mass, the first hard evidence beyond the minimal Standard Model.

title: Electroweak unification is one framework, not one sentence
text: Above roughly 100 GeV, electromagnetism and the weak force are described by an SU(2) times U(1) gauge theory; the W and Z bosons were found in 1983. Feynman was cautious about the word unification: it means one mathematical framework whose couplings split after symmetry breaking, not that the two forces behave alike at low energy.

title: The Standard Model and the Higgs: the part Feynman never saw
text: Feynman died in 1988. The Higgs mechanism and the Higgs boson, found in 2012, became part of the Standard Model after his death; its skeleton is three generations of quarks and leptons, the gauge bosons, and the Higgs field that gives them mass. Neutrino mass still sits outside the minimal model. Calling it Feynman's Standard Model credits him with conclusions he never saw.
aliases: did Feynman know about the Higgs

title: Conservation laws come from symmetry
text: In Volume III, chapter 17, Feynman explains that every conservation law sits on a transformation that changes nothing: time translation gives energy, space translation gives momentum, rotation gives angular momentum. Discrete symmetries such as parity need not hold, and the weak force is the counterexample. When you see a conservation law, ask which symmetry it belongs to.

title: The field is fundamental; particles are excitations of it
text: Feynman's position was not fields between particles but that the field itself is fundamental and a particle is a quantized excitation of it. The field language preserves locality: an influence here reaches there only through neighboring field values. The vacuum is not nothing; it is the field's lowest-energy state and it can fluctuate.

title: Superconductivity is more than zero resistance
text: Below a critical temperature some materials drop to zero resistance and also expel magnetic field from their interior, the Meissner effect. Zero resistance alone does not define the state: a perfect conductor would freeze whatever field it already had, while a superconductor actively pushes the field out with lossless surface currents.

title: Cooper pairs and the energy gap
text: Electrons attract each other very weakly through lattice vibrations and, at low temperature, pair up into Cooper pairs. Pairing opens a gap: breaking a pair costs about twice Delta, so single-particle scattering freezes out and the current stops dissipating. BCS theory made this mechanism precise and related the gap to the critical temperature.
aliases: why does a superconductor have no resistance

title: The Josephson effect makes a macroscopic phase measurable
text: Two superconductors separated by a thin insulator let Cooper pairs tunnel through, carrying a lossless current; apply a DC voltage and the current oscillates at a frequency set by two e V over h. A macroscopic quantum phase becomes a voltage-frequency relation you can measure, the basis of voltage standards and superconducting qubits.

title: Superfluid helium: a quantum liquid with no viscosity
text: Below 2.17 K, liquid helium-4 becomes a superfluid: viscosity is unmeasurably small, it climbs container walls, and it conducts heat extremely well. The two-fluid model describes a normal component and a superfluid component coexisting, the latter being the Bose-condensed part. A superfluid is a macroscopic quantum state in flow, not merely a very thin liquid.
aliases: why does liquid helium climb walls

title: Band structure decides conductors, insulators and semiconductors
text: In a crystal, electrons may occupy only allowed bands, with forbidden gaps between them. What separates a conductor, an insulator and a semiconductor is not whether electrons exist but whether the highest occupied band is partly filled or exactly full. Feynman derived this with the tight-binding approximation in Volume III, chapter 14.

title: A pn junction: one side has electrons, the other holes
text: A p-type semiconductor is doped with acceptors and has many holes; an n-type has donors and many electrons. Join them and carriers diffuse, leaving charged ions behind, which builds a depletion layer and a built-in field that allows current in only one direction. A transistor uses that junction to amplify a weak signal.

title: Phonons are quantized lattice vibrations
text: Atoms in a lattice are never still; they oscillate about equilibrium. Quantize each normal mode and you get phonons. Phonons carry heat and sound, and at low temperature the specific heat of a solid falls as the cube of temperature. Calling a phonon a particle only means its energy and momentum are exchanged in discrete portions.
aliases: how does heat travel through a solid

title: Only electrons near the Fermi surface conduct
text: Electrons in a metal fill states up to the Fermi energy. An electron deep below would need a huge energy kick to change state and cannot respond at room temperature; only the thin shell near the Fermi surface can. That is why the electronic specific heat is proportional to temperature instead of the classical constant.
aliases: why is the electronic specific heat small

title: The partition function is the door to every thermodynamic quantity
text: At temperature T a state of energy E carries weight e to the minus E over kT; summing the weights over all states gives the partition function Z. The free energy is minus kT ln Z, and every other thermodynamic quantity follows by differentiation. The exponential explains why high-energy states are always rare.

title: The three statistics differ on whether particles may share a state
text: Distinguishable particles follow Maxwell-Boltzmann; fermions allow at most one per quantum state; bosons allow any number. At low temperature the differences are macroscopic: fermions pile up to a Fermi sea, bosons crowd into the ground state and condense. Classical statistics is only the high-temperature, low-density limit.

title: A phase transition is an order parameter appearing or vanishing
text: In a phase transition the order parameter goes from zero to nonzero, or back, and some symmetry breaks: water freezes and the crystal picks directions; a magnet cools and the spins pick an axis. Near the critical point the correlation length diverges, so different materials share the same critical exponents.

title: The Ising model: the simplest phase transition
text: Spins take only plus or minus one and couple to nearest neighbors; that is the Ising model. Onsager solved the two-dimensional version exactly in 1944. Its value is not magnetism but demonstration: microscopic rules simple enough to write on one line still produce a macroscopic transition, and critical behavior depends only on dimension and symmetry.

title: Entropy is the logarithm of the number of microscopic states
text: Entropy is k ln W, where W is the number of microscopic states consistent with the given macroscopic conditions. It is a countable number of states, not a vague amount of disorder. The second law says the number of accessible states almost always grows, because the configurations with many states vastly outnumber the rest.

title: Brownian motion is direct evidence of atoms
text: Small particles suspended in a liquid jitter because molecular impacts do not cancel exactly. Einstein showed in 1905 that the mean square displacement grows linearly with time, with a diffusion constant set by temperature and viscosity; Perrin used that relation to measure Avogadro's number. Feynman uses it in Volume I, chapter 41, to show that atoms can be counted without being seen.

title: A ratchet cannot run on a single heat bath
text: A ratchet and pawl look as if they could rectify random molecular impacts into one-way rotation and do work. But the pawl is itself jostled by thermal fluctuations and at equilibrium hops back as often as forward, so the net work is zero. Turning fluctuations into useful work needs a temperature difference, or information.
aliases: why can't a ratchet do work

title: A plasma is a shielded collective gas
text: In a plasma every charge is surrounded by a cloud of opposite charge, with a shielding length set by temperature and density; the whole thing oscillates collectively at the plasma frequency. So it is neither ionized air nor a pile of independent charges: long-range Coulomb is screened to short range, and what remains is governed by collective modes.

title: A laser runs on stimulated emission and population inversion
text: An excited atom struck by a photon of the same frequency emits another photon in phase and in the same direction: stimulated emission. In thermal equilibrium excited atoms are scarce and absorption beats amplification; invert the populations and light is amplified, and a resonator selects the modes, giving coherent light. Feynman used ammonia molecules in Volume III, chapter 9.

title: The refractive index does not come from light being dragged
text: Light slows in a medium not because photons are caught and slowed by atoms. The incoming wave drives the electrons, which reradiate; the reradiated waves add to the original and the phase velocity of the combined wave changes, which is the refractive index. Dispersion is the response failing to keep up. Feynman derives it in Volume I, chapter 31.

title: Least time and diffraction are the same story
text: Feynman derives reflection and refraction from the path of least time in Volume I, chapter 26, but the real mechanism is the path integral: arrows for all paths add, those near the stationary path reinforce, the rest cancel. Diffraction is not light bending around an edge; it is the amplitude redistributing when an aperture restricts the available paths.

title: A single photon either gets through or it doesn't: polarization as a two-state system
text: In the classical picture a polarizer passes only the component of the electric field along its axis, so the intensity falls as cos^2 theta (usually called Malus's law). With one photon there is no field component to split. In Volume III chapter 11 Feynman treats photon polarization as a two-state system: with |x> and |y> as base states, the state turned through the angle theta is |x'> = cos theta |x> + sin theta |y>, and the probability of passing the second polaroid is the square of the amplitude, cos^2 theta. With the first polaroid at 30 degrees a photon gets through 3/4 of the time and 1/4 of the time it is absorbed and heats the polaroid a little. "There is no such thing as 3/4 of a photon. It is either all there, or it isn't there at all." Average over ten billion photons and you recover the classical intensity formula. A piece of calcite that splits light into an x beam and a y beam is the complete analog of a Stern-Gerlach apparatus splitting a beam of silver atoms.

title: Light and electrons are neither classical waves nor classical particles
text: A quantum object is described by a probability amplitude: interference comes from adding amplitudes, and the probability of detection is the squared modulus. So asking whether light is a wave or a particle is the wrong question; ask what the experiment measures. Measuring interference looks at amplitudes; measuring position looks at probabilities.

title: Equivalence principle: gravity and acceleration are locally indistinguishable
text: In a closed elevator the downward feeling could come from Earth's gravity or from the elevator accelerating upward; no local experiment separates them. The equivalence principle turns gravity from a force into spacetime geometry: freely falling objects follow geodesics, and what we call gravity is curvature. The Lectures on Gravitation build from this starting point.

title: Gravitational waves really carry energy: the sticky bead
text: Feynman's argument: put beads with friction on a rod; a passing gravitational wave shakes them and friction makes heat. That heat must come from the wave's energy, or energy conservation fails, and the conclusion needs no coordinate choice because heat is measurable. The argument convinced skeptics that gravitational waves have real physical effects.

title: The horizon is where escape velocity reaches the speed of light
text: The Schwarzschild radius is two G M over c squared; inside it no signal escapes, light included. The horizon is not a material surface but a causal boundary. Black-hole entropy is proportional to horizon area, which became mainstream after Feynman's death; his own worry was whether quantum effects near a black hole destroy information.

title: The universe expands without galaxies flying through space
text: The redshift of distant galaxies comes from the metric itself scaling: the scale factor grows and stretches wavelengths, so one plus z is one over the scale factor. There is no explosion center; every galaxy sees the others receding. This picture is a solution of general relativity, not the Doppler effect applied to galaxies.
aliases: what does it mean that the universe expands

title: There is plenty of room at the bottom: thinking at the nanometer
text: In 1959 Feynman asked what would happen if we could write all twenty-four volumes of the Encyclopaedia Britannica on the head of a pin, build machines from single atoms, make circuits at molecular scale. It sounded like science fiction; today's integrated circuits and molecular machines continue that road. His point was that the laws of physics do not forbid making things smaller.
aliases: plenty of room at the bottom

title: Quantum simulation: use nature to simulate nature
text: In 1982 Feynman argued that a classical computer simulating a quantum system needs resources that grow exponentially with particle number, while a controlled quantum system can simulate another quantum system directly. That is one starting point of quantum computing. The point is not merely speed but a different physical carrier for exponentially many states.

title: Erasing one bit costs kT ln 2 of heat
text: Landauer's principle: erasing one bit dissipates at least kT ln 2. Computation is not pure mathematics; it runs on a physical system and must settle its account with thermodynamics. Reversible computing can avoid dissipation in principle, but error correction, measurement and reset still cost.

title: A rainbow's colours come from dispersion: water bends different colours differently
text: White light refracts entering and leaving water, and water's index of refraction rises with frequency, so blue bends more than red and the colours are spread apart. After one internal reflection inside a raindrop the returning light concentrates in a ring about 42 degrees from the anti-solar point, the primary bow; after two internal reflections it forms the secondary bow near 51 degrees with the colours reversed. Feynman, in Volume I chapter 31 on the origin of the refractive index, notes that the index rises slowly with frequency so blue light is bent more than red; in Volume II chapter 20, on the rainbow, he says that, measured from the direction opposite the sun, the light at 40 degrees is predominantly green and the light at 42 degrees is predominantly red.

title: A rainbow is not seven blocks of colour: the spectrum is continuous
text: Spread sunlight with a prism or a raindrop and you get a continuous spectrum, not seven separate colours. Newton, in the Opticks, divided visible light into red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet as seven principal colour regions and matched them to the seven musical intervals; that is a division and a naming convention, not evidence that nature has only seven colours. He himself wrote that the colours pass into one another in a continual succession with infinitely many intermediate shades. So the question 'why is a rainbow always seven colours' needs rewording: a rainbow is a continuous spectrum laid out by wavelength, and the seven names are a human count.

title: Light bends at a surface by taking the quickest path
text: Light entering glass from air bends. Feynman starts optics from a deeper rule: light takes the path of least time (Fermat's principle). His picture is someone on shore rescuing a girl who has fallen out of a boat: we can run faster than we can swim, so the best route is not the straight line but a little more distance on land and less in the water. Light is slower in water, so the quickest route between two points folds at the surface, and that gives the law of refraction Snell found in 1621, sin theta_i = n sin theta_r. Mirror reflection is another solution of the same principle: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. Light is not pushed at the surface; the whole path is comparing times.

title: The sky is blue because air scatters blue light more
text: Air molecules are driven by the electric field of sunlight and re-radiate in all directions like tiny antennas; that is scattering. In Volume I chapter 32 Feynman works it out: for air the scattering is proportional to the fourth power of the frequency, so light of twice the frequency is scattered sixteen times more intensely. Blue light has about twice the frequency of the red end of the spectrum, so it is scattered far more, and when you look at the sky away from the sun you see blue. The light that comes straight through has had the blue taken out: at sunset it crosses a lot of air, most of the blue is scattered away, and what reaches the eye is yellow-red. He also explains why we see clouds: once water vapor condenses into droplets, the N molecules in a droplet are much closer together than a wavelength and move in phase, so the scattered field is N times and the intensity N^2 times that of one molecule, N times more than the same molecules spread out. This is usually called Rayleigh scattering.

title: A lens focuses light by the least time, again
text: Feynman does not start from rays in Volume I chapter 27: he compares travel times along different paths. For a spherical surface, the extra distance of the near-axial path costs exactly the time saved by travelling more slowly in the glass, giving 1/s + n/s' = (n-1)/R and the general n1/s + n2/s' = (n2-n1)/R. A thin lens works the same way: every path from object point to image point takes equal time, which gives 1/s + 1/s' = 1/f with 1/f = (n-1)(1/R1 - 1/R2). All of this holds in the paraxial approximation only, which is why chapter 27 also treats spherical and chromatic aberration, and resolving power: two points can be told apart only if the longest and shortest times to the image differ by more than one period, t2 - t1 > 1/nu, which is equivalent to the separation D exceeding about lambda/(n sin theta). Feynman's conclusion: "The smallest things that we can see are therefore approximately the wavelength of light"; more magnification does not help. He also notes that the bottom of a pool looks about three quarters of its depth.

title: Synchrotron radiation: light squeezed into a narrow cone
text: A charge moving in a near-light-speed circle does not radiate evenly: the radiation goes into a narrow cone along the instantaneous direction of motion. In Feynman's words, 'These strong electric fields are emitted in a narrow cone in the direction of motion of the charge.' Seen from far away this is not a smooth sweep but sharp pulses, and radiation that would otherwise sit in the radio band is shifted up to visible light or higher, polarised. His numbers: an electron of about 10^9 eV in a 10,000 gauss field has an orbit radius near 3.3 m; Caltech's synchrotron had radius 3.7 m and about 1.5 GeV, with a circumference near 20 m; a billion-electron-volt electron is only about one part in eight million slower than light. The rest of chapter 34 covers bremsstrahlung, the Doppler effect, aberration and the momentum of light p = W/c = hbar k.

title: Colour is in the eye, not the light: three-colour mixing and night vision
text: One colour sensation can come from many different spectra; what matters is how the eye compares its few kinds of receptor. In chapter 35 Feynman says dark-adapted vision is almost entirely rods and bright vision cones, and the eye covers a range of intensity of more than a million to one. On going from bright to dim, different colours swap relative brightness - red and blue paper can reverse - which is the Purkinje effect. He demonstrates colour matching with four projectors: red, green, blue and a white beam with a black spot in the middle. Matching every colour with real primaries needs negative amounts for some colours, so three actual lamps added together do not make every colour.

title: The eye is a piece of brain touching light
text: Feynman's line is: 'The eye is a piece of brain that is touching light, so to speak, on the outside.' The retina does not pass each cell's signal straight to the brain: there are all kinds of cross connections between cells in the layers, so information is already being processed before it leaves the eye. Imaging is mostly the cornea (index about 1.37, water about 1.33, which is why the naked eye sees poorly underwater), with the lens focusing and the iris setting the light level. The pigment that absorbs light in rods is rhodopsin. The bee is a very Feynman example: it can tell apart whites that look identical to us because their ultraviolet reflection differs, it finds the sun from the polarisation of scattered sky light, and the facets of a compound eye are squeezed between angular sampling and diffraction. Feynman estimates the facet size as sqrt(lambda r), about 35 micrometres, against 30 in the book, and calls that rather good agreement.

title: Interference: add the fields of the two sources first, then square
text: In Volume I chapter 29 Feynman starts from one accelerating charge: far away, the electric field is proportional to the acceleration at the retarded time t - r/c and falls off as 1/r, so the energy flow falls as 1/r^2 and the energy inside a given cone is the same at any distance; energy that is radiated away does not come back. With two sources it is the fields that add, not the intensities: A_R^2 = A1^2 + A2^2 + 2 A1 A2 cos(phi2 - phi1), and the last term is the interference term. If it is positive we call it constructive interference, if negative destructive. Feynman complains in passing: "Interference in ordinary language usually suggests opposition or hindrance, but in physics we often do not use language the way it was originally designed!" The phase difference has two parts: the intrinsic phase difference alpha of the oscillators plus 2 pi d sin theta / lambda from the difference in distance. His example is two antennas half a wavelength apart on a north-south line: driven in phase, the intensity east-west is 4 times that of one antenna, zero north-south, and 2 at 30 degrees; reverse the phase of one and the maximum swings from east-west to north-south, so you can broadcast west to Hawaii today and north to Alberta tomorrow without moving an antenna. A quarter-wavelength spacing with a quarter-period delay sends the power one way only, and six antennas in a row driven in phase give 36 times the intensity of one straight ahead.

title: Diffraction: the superposition of many sources
text: Feynman opens Volume I chapter 30 with: "No one has ever been able to define the difference between interference and diffraction satisfactorily. It is just a question of usage, and there is no specific, important physical difference between them." With a few sources, say two, the result is usually called interference; with a large number, diffraction. For n equal oscillators with phase difference phi between neighbours the intensity is I = I0 sin^2(n phi/2) / sin^2(phi/2): the central maximum is n^2 times one oscillator, the first minimum is at phi = 2 pi/n, and the first side maximum is only 4/(9 pi^2) of the peak, less than 5 percent. That is a diffraction grating: a glass sheet with several hundred scratches to the millimeter, with strong beams where d sin theta = m lambda, so longer wavelengths are deflected more and red goes farther out than blue; if the spacing is less than a wavelength only the zero order is left. The resolving power of a grating is lambda/delta lambda = m n, the order times the number of lines. The same arithmetic gives the smallest angle a telescope or parabolic antenna of aperture L can resolve, about lambda/L; for a circular opening it is 1.22 lambda/L, and Feynman remarks that "it seems a little pedantic to put such precision into the resolving power formula." Shine x-rays into a crystal and the intensities of the various orders tell you how the atoms are arranged. For holes in an opaque screen you get the right pattern by treating the holes as uniformly distributed sources, which he admits is "a rather peculiar fact." And the shadow of a straight edge is not a clean cut: exactly at the geometrical shadow edge the intensity is 1/4 of the incident light, with wobbling fringes on the bright side.

title: Polarization: the electric field of light is a vector, and it matters which way it vibrates
text: The electric field of light is perpendicular to the direction of travel and it is a vector; how it vibrates is the polarization. In Volume I chapter 33 Feynman resolves it into x- and y-vibrations: in phase they make linear polarization, equal amplitudes 90 degrees out of phase make circular polarization, anything else is elliptical. Unpolarized light is not another kind of light; its polarization changes faster than the instrument can follow, since one atom radiates for only about 10^-8 seconds. In his words, "light is unpolarized only if we are unable to find out whether the light is polarized or not." Polaroid is a thin layer of small crystals of herapathite (a salt of iodine and quinine), all aligned, which absorb vibrations in one direction only: for light polarized at angle theta to the pass direction the amplitude is cut by cos theta and the intensity by cos^2 theta. Two crossed sheets pass nothing, yet a third sheet at 45 degrees placed between them lets some light through; he leaves that "as an exercise for the student." Skylight scattered at 90 degrees to the sunbeam is polarized. Light reflected from glass is completely polarized when the reflected and refracted beams form a right angle (Brewster's angle), because the reflected beam is really re-radiated by charges driven in the material, and a charge does not radiate along its own line of motion. A birefringent crystal has different indexes for the two polarizations, and the right thickness makes a quarter-wave plate; Iceland spar shows everything doubled; molecules without reflection symmetry, as in corn syrup, rotate the plane of polarization (optical activity). At normal incidence water reflects only about 2 percent of the light: (n-1)^2/(n+1)^2 with n = 4/3.

title: Dielectric polarization: the charges in an insulator are pulled apart a little
text: Put a sheet of glass or lucite between the plates of a parallel-plate capacitor and Faraday found the capacitance goes up, by a factor kappa that depends only on the material: that is the dielectric constant, and for a vacuum kappa is one. An insulator does not conduct, so why is there any electrical effect at all? Feynman's answer: every atom in the material is pulled into an induced dipole, its positive and negative charge centers displaced a little. The dipole moment per unit volume is the polarization vector P; for a slab in a parallel-plate capacitor the surfaces show a polarization charge density sigma_pol = P, opposite in sign to the free charge on the plates, so the field inside is reduced: E = (sigma_free - P)/epsilon_0, and the capacitance becomes kappa epsilon_0 A/d. For fields that are not too large, P is proportional to E, written P = chi epsilon_0 E, with chi the electric susceptibility, and kappa = 1 + chi. Where P varies from place to place there is also a volume charge density rho_pol = -div P. The vector D = epsilon_0 E + P was introduced historically to keep the equations looking simple: div D = rho_free, D = epsilon E with epsilon = kappa epsilon_0, the permittivity. Feynman warns that D = epsilon E describes matter, matter is extremely complicated, and the relation fails for large fields; it is an approximation like Hooke's law and "cannot be a deep and fundamental equation". The fundamental equations are always the ones in terms of E and all the charges. This is polarization of matter by an electric field, not the vacuum polarization of quantum field theory.
